h1: Boeing 777: The First Jetliner Designed Entirely on Computer
description: The Boeing 777 first flew on June 12, 1994, as the first jetliner designed 100 percent digitally. Specs, the 777X with folding wingtips and sources.
intro: The Boeing 777 is a long-range widebody airliner with two engines, and the first jetliner designed 100 percent digitally. Boeing's engineers preassembled the whole airplane as a three-dimensional computer model instead of building a costly full-scale mock-up. It first flew on June 12, 1994.

It was Boeing's first entirely new airplane in more than a decade. United Airlines launched the program with an order in October 1990 and began 777 passenger service in June 1995, on a route between London and Washington, DC. The new jet was bigger than any twinjet or trijet before it, but smaller than the [747](/aircraft/boeing-747).

The family grew in steps. The larger 777-300 was first delivered to Cathay Pacific in June 1998, and the long-range 777-300ER rolled out on November 14, 2002. The 777-200LR, which Boeing billed as the world's longest-range commercial airplane, and the 777 Freighter completed the lineup. Boeing builds every model at its factory in Everett, Washington.
whyItMatters: The 777 is a showcase for the turbofan. Airlines could pick engines from three makers: Pratt & Whitney, Rolls-Royce or GE. GE's GE90 was the first airliner engine with composite fan blades. The new 777X uses the GE9X, whose 134-inch fan sends about 10 times as much air around the engine's core as through it. The [jet engines guide](/learn/how-jet-engines-work) explains why fans that big save fuel.

It also became a fixture of long-haul flying. By December 2025, nearly 100 customers had ordered more than 2,300 777s, and Boeing had delivered more than 1,750. By Boeing's count, the fleet had carried nearly 4 billion passengers and flown 49 billion miles, and it was making nearly 1,800 flights a day.

Before any passenger boarded, Boeing tested the structure hard. A 1995 static test showed it could bear 150 percent of the highest loads any airplane should meet in service. A fatigue test that ended in 1997 then ran an airframe through 120,000 simulated flight cycles, or three design lifetimes. The [turbulence guide](/learn/is-turbulence-dangerous) explains why such margins matter, and [Boeing vs Airbus](/learn/boeing-vs-airbus) compares the two makers' families.
facts: The 777 was the first airplane to have a rose named after it: a deep purple-red variety with a citrus-like scent, bred by Western Independent Nurseries of Olympia, Washington.

The 777-9's wingtips fold. Its span is 235 feet 5 inches (71.8 m) with the tips extended for flight. Folded on the ground, it shrinks to 212 feet 9 inches (64.8 m), about the same as a 777-300ER's span.
At 251 feet 9 inches (76.7 m) long, the 777-9 seats 375 to 450 passengers in two classes, by Boeing's figures.
Boeing launched the 777X at the Dubai Airshow in November 2013 with 259 commitments from four customers. As of October 2026, the 777-9 was in flight testing, with first delivery planned for 2027.
The GE9X holds a world record of 134,300 pounds of thrust, yet it has only 16 composite fan blades, six fewer than the GE90.
